title: WITAWITADD - Escapism!
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hyisCTgnS0g

Recorded in late March 2020, this is the pandemic episode, and Daniel (@dungeondive) doesn't pretend otherwise — he's asthmatic, the world is frightening, and he needs escapism more than ever. What follows is a defence of it as a mental-health practice rather than an indulgence.

He starts with childhood: teachers told his parents he lived inside his head too much, and he doesn't accept the premise that either that or an overactive imagination is possible. There's a lovely detail — shown a picture of a fire hydrant in a kindergarten aptitude test, he identified it as R2-D2. It also explains his indifference to euros: economic simulation and farming are reality, and he wants a break from reality, not a chore as a hobby.

The observation that lands hardest is that escapism starts long before play. Browsing Kickstarter or BGG for something to buy is already surveying worlds you might visit. Opening a box is opening a door. He'll pull a game off the shelf, set up the board, read the flavour text and never play it. Dungeon Degenerates, Folklore, Mice and Mystics, Shadows of Brimstone, Legends of Andor and Machina Arcana all get named as worlds worth being inside.

He's honest about the balance point — shirk your health or your people and it stops being healthy — and he closes by reaching out to anyone whose gaming was social, now cut off, and naming that as grief.

----

Has a game ever done real work for you during a bad stretch? And do you get some of that escape just from setting a game up and reading it, without ever playing?
